summary: The appointed makers receive such abundant offerings that they report a surplus and Moses stops further contributions. The construction account then describes the joined linen curtains and outer coverings, the wooden frame with metal bases and bars, and the veil and entrance screen of the sanctuary.
whyItMatters: The earlier command becomes a completed sequence of material work, supported by a community that has supplied more than enough. Repeated measurements and joins let the reader compare the built tent with the earlier design.

context.author: Exodus does not name its final author. It records Moses writing particular covenant material; traditional Mosaic attribution and modern accounts of composition are distinguished in the book briefing.
context.audience: Israel remembering its rescue from Egypt and its obligations as a covenant community. The chapter does not identify an individual dedicatee.
context.date: The narrative places these events at Sinai after the departure from Egypt. The date of the events and the history of the book’s composition are separate, debated questions.
context.setting: The Israelite camp as the sanctuary makers begin using the collected gifts after covenant renewal.
context.literaryForm: A report of sufficient supplies followed by a detailed construction narrative for the tent enclosure.

before.text: Men and women have brought willing gifts, skilled women have spun material, and Bezalel and Oholiab have been named as makers and teachers. The work can now begin.

here.text: A surplus first brings the collection to an end; the narrative then follows the actual fabrication of the tent's layers, frame, and hangings.

after.text: The next construction report turns to the ark and its cover, table, lamp stand, incense altar, and the sacred mixtures.

outline.heading: The workers receive enough and more
outline.note: The makers report the surplus and Moses restrains further giving.

outline.heading: The joined inner curtains
outline.note: Ten decorated linen panels and gold clasps form one tabernacle unit.

outline.heading: Goats’ hair and outer coverings
outline.note: Eleven larger curtains are joined, with skins covering the tent.

outline.heading: Boards and supporting sockets
outline.note: The sides and rear corners take shape through upright acacia boards and silver bases.

outline.heading: Bars and gold covering
outline.note: The frame is joined and covered with its prescribed metalwork.

outline.heading: The veil and entrance screen
outline.note: Distinct hangings and supporting pillars complete the enclosure’s partitions.

keyVerses.text: They spoke to Moses, saying, “The people have brought much more than enough for the service of the work which Yahweh commanded to make.”
keyVerses.why: The working craftsmen report the actual sufficiency of the supplied materials.

keyVerses.text: Moses gave a commandment, and they caused it to be proclaimed throughout the camp, saying, “Let neither man nor woman make anything else for the offering for the sanctuary.” So the people were restrained from bringing.
keyVerses.why: Moses ends the collection once its stated purpose is met.

keyVerses.text: He made fifty clasps of gold, and coupled the curtains to one another with the clasps: so the tabernacle was a unit.
keyVerses.why: The account explicitly reports the separate curtains becoming one tabernacle unit.

questions.question: What qualifies the people Moses calls to the work?
questions.answer: The opening joins God-given wisdom and understanding with hearts stirred to undertake the task. Skill and willingness both matter in the described group, and Bezalel and Oholiab work with others rather than replacing them.

questions.question: How does Moses learn that the collection can stop?
questions.answer: The people keep bringing gifts each morning, and the makers leave their work to report that they have more than enough. The stop order responds to the workers' assessment of what the assigned construction needs.

questions.question: Why does the west end have eight boards when verse 27 names six?
questions.answer: The account first counts six boards for the rear, then adds two boards for the rear corners. It totals these as eight boards with sixteen silver sockets, two sockets beneath each board. The corner pieces explain the change in the count.

questions.question: What do the “clasps” accomplish?
questions.answer: They fasten opposite loops on the curtain sets, joining separate panels into one enclosure. The linen system uses gold clasps, while the goats' hair covering uses bronze, preserving the difference between the layers.

questions.question: What is the relationship between the twenty boards and forty sockets?
questions.answer: Each board has two tenons and two silver sockets, so each long side's twenty boards is supported by forty bases. The repeated pairing links the number of bases directly to the design of the upright boards.

questions.question: What does the middle bar do in the construction account?
questions.answer: It passes through the boards from one end to the other among the bars that join the sides. The narrative then records gold over the boards and bars and gold rings to receive them, attending to both connection and surface.

questions.question: Are the veil and door screen identical?
questions.answer: They share colored fabric and fine linen, but the veil has cherubim and four silver-based pillars, while the entrance screen has five pillars with bronze bases. The completed work preserves two separate thresholds with different fittings.

glossary.def: Fasteners that join the loops of adjacent curtain groups into one structure.
The paired projecting joins by which each board fits into its bases.
The metal bases supporting the boards and pillars.
